title: The Alternator That Wasn't Broken (tree pilot)
complaintTemplate: CUST STATES: 'charging system STILL not right.' Two alternators in 6 months for low charging voltage — he watches a plug-in voltmeter read 12.9V while driving, 14.6V other times. Batteries keep dying young. Says it all started right after a parts-store battery got put in.

faultSeeds.internalNote: Nothing electrical is broken. The parts-store battery was never registered to the BMS, so the ECM's charge strategy still runs the OLD battery's aged profile and chronically undercharges the new one (12.9V commanded) — reads as 'low charging' and kills batteries young. Commanded==actual, so both replaced alternators were innocent. Correct fix: register the battery, verify commanded climbs, replace NOTHING. Confirming test: the registration/battery-profile check.

activeFaults.label: new battery never registered to the BMS (charge strategy running the old battery's profile)

resultOverrides.act_scan_pids: Commanded 12.9V, actual 12.9V — output is matching command exactly; the alternator is delivering what the ECM asks for. BMS-reported state of charge: 55%.
resultOverrides.act_check_registration: Battery registration: never performed. The stored profile still carries the age and capacity of the unit that was replaced months ago.
resultOverrides.act_inspect_sensor: The battery current sensor, its ground eyelet, and its connector are clean; voltage drop across its ground is 0.02V under load — in spec.
resultOverrides.act_battery_test: Date code: about 2 months old. Load-tests strong at 95%, plates healthy — a genuinely fresh battery. The BMS is reporting it at 55% state of charge.

faultSeeds.internalNote: The battery current sensor (IBS) clamped on the negative battery cable has a corroded ground/connector, so it feeds the strategy bad current/SOC data — the charge command wanders and undercharges. A registration alone will NOT hold, because the sensor keeps lying. Correct fix: repair the sensor ground/connection (then register). Confirming test: inspect / voltage-drop the sensor.

activeFaults.label: corroded battery current sensor ground on the negative cable

resultOverrides.act_scan_pids: Commanded voltage swings 11.9–15.1V with no pattern; actual tracks it. BMS state-of-charge reading jumps around erratically.
resultOverrides.act_check_registration: Registration shows performed and current. The state-of-charge history is present but noisy.
resultOverrides.act_inspect_sensor: The battery current sensor's ground eyelet is green and corroded; voltage drop across its ground reads 0.6V under load, spec near zero. The connector pins are dark.
resultOverrides.act_battery_test: Recent date code, load-tests okay. But the live state-of-charge and current values on the scan tool jump around impossibly.

faultSeeds.internalNote: This time the alternator IS bad — commanded 14.6V but actual only 13.0V at the B+ post under load. The strategy is asking correctly; the hardware underdelivers. The ONLY way to know is comparing commanded vs actual — the dash voltmeter can't tell this from the other two seeds. A blind swap physically fixes it but is a lucky, undiagnosed fix. Confirming test: the commanded-vs-actual scan.

resultOverrides.act_scan_pids: Commanded 14.6V, but actual only 13.0V at the B+ post under load. Output is falling well short of command.
resultOverrides.act_inspect_sensor: The battery current sensor, ground, and connector all check out — voltage drop 0.02V, readings steady.
resultOverrides.act_battery_test: A few months old and a bit worn from months of undercharge, but still serviceable.

nodes.prompt: Two alternators in six months, batteries dying young, a customer glued to a plug-in voltmeter — and it all started after a parts-store battery. Where do you start?

options.label: Scan the charging system — commanded vs. actual voltage — before touching a part
Start at the battery current sensor clamped on the negative battery cable
Pull it in and run a proper workup
The meter reads 12.9V — that's low. Put a third alternator in

nodes.prompt: Back at the truck. What's your next move?

options.label: Scan commanded vs. actual charge voltage + BMS state-of-charge
Check whether the new battery was ever registered to the BMS
Inspect and voltage-drop the battery current sensor (on the negative cable) and its ground
Assess the battery — load test, date code, and wear
Watch the customer's dash voltmeter
Unplug the BMS to force steady charging
Put in a third alternator
I'm ready to commit to a root cause

nodes.prompt: You put the scan tool on the charging PIDs — commanded charge voltage, actual charge voltage, and BMS state of charge — and drive it.

options.label: Log it — pull the BMS registration / battery profile too
Log it and inspect the battery current sensor
I've got the discriminating reading — commit

nodes.prompt: You pull the BMS battery-registration status and the stored battery profile.

options.label: Log it and commit to a root cause
Cross-check the sensor and battery first

nodes.prompt: You inspect and voltage-drop the battery current sensor clamped on the negative battery cable — its ground eyelet, pigtail, and connector.

options.label: Log it and commit to a root cause
Cross-check the scan data first

nodes.prompt: You assess the installed battery — load test, date code, and state of wear.

options.label: Log it and keep testing the system
Battery's the story — replace it and release

nodes.prompt: You watch the customer's plug-in voltmeter: 12.9V cruising, 14.6V at other times — exactly what he reported, and exactly what variable charging is supposed to do. The meter reads moments; it can't tell strategy from fault.
nodes.continueLabel: Right — the meter can't diagnose this. Back to the truck.

nodes.prompt: You unplug the BMS. The alternator drops into a steady ~13.5V fallback and the swings stop — but you've set a charging-system code and crippled the strategy. It hides the question instead of answering it.

options.label: Reconnect it — that's not a diagnosis. Back to the truck.
Leave it defeated and call it fixed

nodes.prompt: Commit to a specific root cause. What gets done — and what, if anything, gets replaced?

options.label: Register the new battery to the BMS and clear the stale profile — replace nothing
It's the battery current sensor — repair its ground/connection on the negative cable, then register
It's the alternator — replace it
Batteries keep dying — just put another battery in and send it
Leave the BMS defeated so it charges steady

nodes.prompt: You run the battery registration / relearn so the strategy drops the stale profile, then drive it and re-check commanded voltage against actual.
nodes.continueLabel: Re-check commanded vs. actual and release

nodes.prompt: You repair the battery current sensor's ground eyelet and connector on the negative cable, register the battery, then re-check commanded vs. actual.
You install a replacement alternator and re-check commanded vs. actual at the B+ post.
You put another battery in and send it.

Commanded and actual track on a known-good, registered battery, state of charge re-baselines on the drive, and the swings are normal strategy again. Fixed — and you can show the customer why on the scan tool.
It's back on the next visit. The real fault was never addressed.

The BMS is unplugged, so it charges dumb and steady — and there's a charging-system code on the dash now. You didn't fix it, you blindfolded it. It comes back worse, and the next tech inherits your code.
